title: Design a chat app
dek: Zotato Chat lets friends plan dinner together: one-to-one chats and small groups, messages that arrive in a blink, ticks that show they were delivered and read, and nothing lost when a phone drops off the network in a lift.

items: Phones keep a connection open to a gateway server, so messages can be pushed to them instantly. A registry remembers which gateway each person is on.
A message is saved before it's acknowledged. Then it's passed to the gateways of everyone in the conversation, or to a phone notification for anyone offline.
Every conversation numbers its messages: 41, 42, 43. That gives one order for everyone, and lets a phone that was offline ask for "everything after 42".
Phones attach their own id to each message they send, so a resend after a bad network is saved once, not twice.
Ticks are just more small messages: "delivered up to 45", "read up to 45".
Send and receive text messages, one-to-one and in groups of up to a few hundred.
A message reaches an online person within a second; an offline person gets a notification and sees it when they open the app.
Delivered and read ticks; the same order for everyone in a conversation.
Out of scope here: photos and voice notes (see the photo-sharing question), calls, and end-to-end encryption, which we'll note where it changes things.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: Under a second from send to the other phone, when both are online
A message that got its first tick is never lost
Everyone in a conversation sees the same order
1 crore people a day, 40 messages each, about 30 lakh online at the evening peak

items: Messages: 1 crore × 40 is 40 crore a day, about 4,600 a second on average. Evenings run about three times that: plan for 15,000 a second.
Connections: 30 lakh phones online at the peak. If one gateway holds about a lakh open connections, that's 30 gateways; run 45 so one can fail without the rest filling up.
Storage: about 200 bytes a message is 80 GB a day, around 29 TB a year. Split by conversation from the start.
Registry: 30 lakh entries of "person → gateway" is a few hundred MB, comfortably in Redis.
Conversation: `id`, `members`, `last_seq` (the number of its newest message).
Message: `conversation_id`, `seq`, `sender_id`, `client_id` (the phone's own id for it), `text`, `sent_at`.
Receipt: per member and conversation, `delivered_up_to` and `read_up_to`.
Registry entry: person → gateway, with a short expiry that the gateway keeps renewing.

body.label: Over the open connection
body.say: Send a message and get back its number. Receive messages as they arrive. Say how far you've read. After reconnecting, ask for everything after the last number you have.

body.cap: The chat service numbers the message, saves it, asks the registry where each other member is connected, and hands it to their gateway, which sends it down the open connection. Anyone offline gets a phone notification instead.

body.x: Gateways only hold connections: they don't decide anything, so any of them can take any phone. The chat service does the numbering and saving, and can be scaled separately from the number of connections.

body.name: First try
body.what: The app asks the server "anything new?" every few seconds.
body.avoid: Messages arrive seconds late, and 30 lakh phones asking every 3 seconds is 10 lakh requests a second, almost all of them answered "nothing new". Batteries suffer too.
body.ex: Ananya asks "8 pm?" and Rohit's reply shows up 3 seconds after he sent it.
body.like: Walking to the letterbox every few minutes in case a letter came.

body.name: Better
body.what: Each phone keeps one connection open to a gateway (a WebSocket). The server sends messages down it the moment they're saved. A registry maps each person to their gateway.
body.use: Instant delivery, and no traffic when nothing is happening apart from a small heartbeat.
body.avoid: Gateways hold state (open connections), so deploys and crashes drop lakhs of them at once. Phones must reconnect with a random delay, or they all come back in the same second.
body.ex: Rohit's reply reaches Ananya's open connection a few hundred milliseconds after he taps Send.
body.like: Keeping a phone line open with a friend, instead of calling every few minutes.

items: The chat service bumps the conversation's `last_seq` and saves the message in one write to the store. A unique key on (conversation, number) turns any double into an error, even if two servers briefly handle the same conversation.

The first tick means "saved", and comes only after the save is on more than one machine. If the phone gets no tick, it sends again with the same `client_id`; the server sees it already has that one and returns the same number (a unique key on conversation + `client_id` makes this check safe).

Delivery to other members happens after the save. If a gateway is down at that moment, nothing is lost: the message is in storage, and the member will fetch it by number. Phones also watch the numbers: if Rohit's phone gets #47 while it has only #45, it asks for "everything after 45" straight away. And until a member's "delivered up to" reaches the new number, the server retries the push.

body.cap: Rohit's phone has messages up to #42, then drops off. When it reconnects it asks for everything after 42 and gets #43, #44 and #45, in order. A resend carries the phone's own message id, so it's saved once.

items: A group message is saved once, then sent to each member's gateway. For a group of 200, that's 200 small deliveries, which is fine.
For very large groups (lakhs of members, like a broadcast channel), don't push to everyone: notify, and let phones fetch by number when they open it.
Ticks in groups: "delivered" when every member's phone has it, "read" when everyone has read it. Keep `delivered_up_to` and `read_up_to` per member and work it out from those.

A gateway crashes: its phones reconnect to others after a random short wait, register again, and send their last number for every conversation in one request, getting back only the ones with new messages.
The registry entry is stale (the phone moved gateways): the delivery fails, the phone's new registration replaces the old entry (or it expires), and the phone's sync on reconnect fills the gap.
A storage machine is slow: sends wait for the save, because the first tick promises the message is safe. Show "sending…" rather than a false tick.
Junior / mid: open connections instead of asking repeatedly, save then deliver, notifications for offline people, a table of messages per conversation.
Senior: the registry, numbers per conversation, sync after reconnecting, resends saved once, ticks.
Lead: reconnect storms after a deploy, very large groups, splitting storage by conversation, where end-to-end encryption changes what the server can see.
"End-to-end encryption?" The server stores and passes on messages it can't read. Numbering, ticks and sync still work; search and moderation on the server don't.
"Show 'typing…'?" Send it over the open connection without saving it. If it's lost, nobody minds.
"Several devices for one person?" Register each device; deliver to all of them; each syncs from its own last number.
"Delete for everyone?" A new message that says "remove #45", so phones that sync later get the delete in order.
"How do you test it?" Kill gateways in the middle of a busy group chat and check that every phone ends with the same messages, in the same order, with no duplicates.

body.x: Gateways are servers behind a load balancer, and the first lesson is the same as any server's: one isn't enough.

practice.brief: Each test sends chat messages. A message is acknowledged once it is safely in a durable queue (a log kept on several machines); workers then number it and save it (2 queries) and deliver it to the other phones. Your Clients' own rate is ignored.

checks.label: Messages reach online users over connections that stay open
Messages are kept in a store built for very many writes, split by conversation and in time order

tests.name: The evening peak
tests.desc: 15,000 messages a second at 9 pm. Each must be saved before its first tick.

tests.name: Diwali wishes
tests.desc: At 8 pm on Diwali everyone wishes everyone: 30,000 messages a second for 15 minutes.

tests.name: A server group dies
tests.desc: At the peak (15,000 a second) the busiest group of servers crashes; it is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of messages still succeed
No server group that every request depends on (no single point of failure)

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the busiest database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

checks.label: At least 99.8% of messages still succeed
Every database has a standby in another zone (Multi-AZ)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (5,000 a second). Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails, like a memory limit.

tests.name: Send a message
tests.desc: u1 sends "hi" in chat c1. The reply comes once the message is safely in the durable queue; workers number it, store it and deliver it a moment later.

est.label: Phones connected at peak

api.label: Fetch messages after a sequence number

decisions.q: How does a message reach a friend who is online?
options: It's pushed the moment it arrives, over a connection kept open
Their app asks the server for new messages every few seconds
Their app holds a request open until a message arrives, then reopens it
decisions.why: Polling either delays messages or floods the servers with empty requests. Long polling works but reconnects after every message. An open WebSocket delivers in milliseconds and costs almost nothing while quiet.

decisions.q: Messages in a chat must show in the same order for everyone. How?
options: Sort them by the time on the sender's phone
A sequence number per conversation, given by the server
Sort them by the time each one reaches the database server
decisions.why: Phone clocks disagree, and arrival times differ between database machines. A per-conversation number from the server gives one order that every device agrees on.

decisions.q: The friend is offline. What happens to the message?
options: The server keeps retrying their connection until it gets through
It's held on the sender's phone until the friend comes online again
It's stored, then delivered when they reconnect, with a push meanwhile
decisions.why: Store and forward: the message is safe on the server, and a push notification tells them to open the app. Endless retries waste servers, and keeping it on the sender's phone fails if that phone goes offline.

decisions.q: How are messages split across machines?
options: By conversation id, sorted by time inside each conversation
By sender id, so each person's sent messages stay together on one machine
By message id, spread evenly over all the machines
decisions.why: Opening a chat reads one conversation's latest messages. Keeping each conversation together and in time order makes that one quick read; splitting by sender or message id scatters a chat over many machines.

hints.x: The first tick means "saved". What has to be true about a message after that tick?
40 crore messages a day, evenings about 3× the average. And how many phones hold a connection open?
Phones keep a WebSocket to a gateway. Over plain HTTP: POST a message, GET messages after the last sequence number you have.
15,000 messages a second is 30,000 queries: more than one database. Split by conversation across several.
Save first, deliver after. A Queue between the gateways and the delivery workers absorbs the Diwali burst.
Two groups at every server layer, Multi-AZ databases: a ticked message is never lost.

wrong.name: One server group
wrong.why: When it crashes, nothing answers for 5 minutes.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: A crash keeps it down for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: No queue
wrong.why: The burst hits the database directly and crashes it.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Passes the load but costs far more than the traffic needs.

wrong.name: Right sizes, general parts
wrong.why: The sizes and redundancy are right, but no component does the job this problem turns on, so the design would carry the traffic without doing what was asked.

wrong.name: Messages without their chat
wrong.why: Messages are stored without the chat they belong to, so a chat's history can't be found.
